ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
Florian has seven pieces of wire of lengths $1 \mathrm{~cm}, 2 \mathrm{~cm}, 3 \mathrm{~cm}, 4 \mathrm{~cm}, 5 \mathrm{~cm}, 6 \mathrm{~cm}$ and $7 \mathrm{~cm}$. He uses some of those pieces to form a wire model of a cube with side length 1. He does not want any overlapping wire parts. What is the smallest number of wire pieces that he can use?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The attached figure is a cube wireframe diagram; it can be seen that it has front and back two square faces, totaling 8 vertices and 12 edges. According to the method draft, label the vertices of the front square as A-B-C-D-A, label the vertices of the back square as E-F-G-H-E, and the connecting edges are A-E, B-F, C-G, D-H. Reasoning: Each edge length of the cube is 1 cm, so a complete cube wireframe needs to cover 12 unit edges, with total length 12 cm. Since overlap is not allowed, each edge must be covered exactly once by some piece of wire. Lower bound: At each vertex of the cube, 3 edges meet. If a piece of wire only passes through a vertex, it will use two adjacent edges at that vertex; but 3 is odd, so at each vertex, there must be at least one wire endpoint stopping there. Therefore 8 vertices require at least 8 wire endpoints. Each piece of wire has 2 endpoints, so at least 8/2 = 4 pieces of wire are needed. Feasible construction: Use four pieces of wire with lengths 5 cm, 4 cm, 2 cm, and 1 cm. Place them along the following non-overlapping paths respectively: length 5: E-A-B-F-G-C; length 4: A-D-H-E-F; length 2: B-C-D; length 1: G-H. The edges covered by these paths, taken together, are exactly the 12 edges of the cube, each edge covered once, with no overlap. Therefore 4 pieces of wire can do it. So the minimum number is 4.

method.method_draft: Label the cube vertices from the image as front square A-B-C-D-A and back square E-F-G-H-E, with connecting edges A-E, B-F, C-G, D-H. From the text, each cube edge is 1 cm, so the wire model consists of 12 unit edges and total wire length 12 cm. For a lower bound, observe physically at each cube corner three wire edge-segments meet. If a piece merely passes through a corner, it uses two incident segments there; because 3 is odd, at least one wire piece must end at every one of the 8 cube corners. Since each wire piece has two ends, at least 8/2 = 4 pieces are necessary. For achievability, use four available pieces with lengths 5, 4, 2, and 1. Route them along edge-disjoint paths: length 5 along E-A-B-F-G-C; length 4 along A-D-H-E-F; length 2 along B-C-D; length 1 along G-H. These paths cover all 12 cube edges exactly once with no overlapping wire parts, so 4 pieces suffice and the minimum is 4.

Place them respectively along the following non-overlapping paths: length 5: E-A-B-F-G-C; length 4: A-D-H-E-F; length 2: B-C-D; length 1: G-H. The edges covered by these paths together are exactly the 12 edges of the cube, each edge covered once, with no overlap. Therefore 4 pieces of wire can do it.

So the minimum number is 4.
